text: When a pet needs more of a medication a doctor already prescribed, fill it as a refill. It copies the doctor's directions exactly, and keeps the count of refills right.
Maple is here for a recheck, and her family wants more Carprofen. In Checkout, click Refills.
Every prescription on file is listed, including the ones that came over from eVet. Each shows the refills left, who prescribed it, and the directions.
Apoquel has no refills left. That one needs a new script from the doctor, so it isn't a refill.
Carprofen has two left. Click Use this refill.
Open the line to see it.
It's a refill of that prescription, with who prescribed it and what's left.
The doctor's directions are right here, and they're locked, so nobody can change them on a refill.
Say the doctor wants Maple on different directions today. Don't edit the refill. Click New directions.
This stops the old prescription. Its refills go to zero, so nobody fills it again with the old directions.
This line becomes a new script for the visit's doctor, and the doctor gets the production.
Click Stop refills and write a new script.
The new script starts with Carprofen's usual directions from the catalog. The doctor checks them, sets the refills, and approves it like any new script.
Her vaccines from eVet are on her chart too. Click View details.
Here's her rabies dose from eVet, with the vet who gave it.
To reprint the rabies certificate, click Print document,
then Rabies certificate.
It's signed by the vet who gave the dose, and shows their license number.
Client liaisons: refills are the one script you can add yourself, because you're only copying directions a vet already wrote. New directions is for the doctor or a tech.
Two mistakes to avoid: changing directions on a refill, and changing the vet on a certificate. For new directions, stop the old script and write a new one, and let the dose decide the vet.
